ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Weld Inspection | Fort Worth, TX
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection in Fort Worth, TX for plants, rail-served sites, gas facilities and fabricators. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Weld Inspection in Fort Worth, Texas
ut.html:
If you operate steel equipment in Fort Worth, Atlantis NDT can mobilize a Level II technician to measure what is left of the wall and to examine welds ultrasonically. We perform ultrasonic thickness testing on tanks, vessels, piping and structural members, and UT weld inspection with angle-beam shear-wave probes, then issue a report that your inspector or engineer can file. Send the equipment list, code and access details through the quote request form; we reply within one business day.

Where UT is used around Fort Worth

Fort Worth is a logistics, aerospace and energy city, and UT follows the steel in each. A major freight railroad is run from the city, and Tarrant County is crossed by mainlines, yards and intermodal terminals. The AllianceTexas development in the north of the city covers about 27,000 acres, with an airport that ranks among the larger cargo airports in the country, distribution buildings, a rail-served inland port and manufacturing plants. Each of these has steel to measure: crane rails and runway beams in industrial buildings, tank and piping systems for fuel and utilities, loading structures, and heavy steel racking.

Aerospace and defense are major employers. Aircraft manufacturers and their suppliers use ground-support equipment, jigs, pressure vessels for test and utility services, and plant piping for compressed air, nitrogen and hydraulics. New hangar and maintenance construction at the airport brings structural steel and fabricated platforms. West and south of the city, the Barnett Shale built a gas-gathering network of pipelines, compressor stations, separators and tanks, and although drilling has slowed, those assets still need periodic wall thickness checks. The nearby Arlington assembly plant and its suppliers add stamping presses, pressure receivers and process piping.

Thickness surveys: method and judgment

A thickness survey is a map of remaining wall. The technician selects a dual-element probe, which suits corroded and pitted surfaces because the transmit and receive crystals are angled to share a short sound path. He calibrates on a step block of the same alloy covering the thickness range, confirms the zero point, and checks again at the end of the job. On gas-gathering piping and tanks the measurement grid usually follows the owner's inspection plan, with readings at condition monitoring locations marked on the isometric.

The A-scan stays on the display. A digital gauge can lock onto a lamination mid-wall and report a thickness that is not the back wall, or it can double on thin steel. Reading the waveform catches both. Where the outer surface is rough, we dress a small patch to bright metal and record that the reading came from a prepared spot. Lines in service at elevated temperature need high-temperature probes and couplant, and the reading is adjusted for temperature. ASME Section V Article 5, ASTM E797 and our thickness measurement requirements guide give the background; the national page on ultrasonic testing services explains the full scope.

Shear-wave examination of welds

Weld examination uses an angled probe, typically 45, 60 or 70 degrees, to send shear waves obliquely through the joint. The technician builds a reference level from side-drilled holes in a calibration block of similar acoustic character, then scans from both sides of the weld where access allows, moving the probe in a raster pattern to cover the full volume. A reflector is classified by amplitude, position and the way the echo moves as the probe moves: planar flaws such as cracks and lack of fusion produce sharp, directional echoes, while slag and porosity produce more rounded, less directional ones.

In Fort Worth this serves structural fabricators building to AWS D1.1, pressure-equipment shops working to ASME Section VIII and B31.3, and operators who have made repairs to pipe or vessel welds. Where the code allows UT instead of radiography, the owner, engineer and authorized inspector agree it before work begins. The ultrasonic testing guide explains how the technique is applied.

What UT can and cannot see

Ultrasound reads through the wall, so UT is the conventional method that looks inside. It finds wall loss from corrosion and erosion, laminations, and internal weld flaws that reflect the beam back toward the probe. It is weak where sound cannot enter or return. Scale and thick coating prevent contact, cast and austenitic material scatters the beam, a weld crown can block probe positions, and a flaw parallel to the beam hardly reflects at all. UT also does not replace a surface method for fine surface-breaking cracks, especially on rough surfaces.

  • Contact: poor coupling gives readings that look steady but are wrong, so surface preparation is part of the work.
  • Geometry: nozzles, tees and tight bends limit where an angle beam can scan.
  • Material: coarse grain in castings and stainless welds causes noise that hides small reflectors.

For surface cracks at carbon-steel weld toes, add magnetic particle testing in Fort Worth; for stainless or aluminum, add penetrant testing in Fort Worth.

Codes, acceptance and the Texas framework

The governing code sets the procedure and the acceptance limits. Pressure vessels in service fall under API 510, piping under API 570 and tanks under API 653, where the owner's authorized inspector is responsible and we supply the measurements and weld data. New construction and repair use ASME Section VIII Division 1, where Appendix 12 covers ultrasonic examination of welds, or B31.3, where paragraph 344.6 and Table 341.3.2 set the examination and acceptance. Structural steel follows AWS D1.1, and state-funded bridge steel follows AWS D1.5. Pipelines carrying gas or hazardous liquids come under 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195, with API 1104 for girth welds, and the Railroad Commission of Texas oversees intrastate pipeline safety.

The state boiler program, run by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation under Health and Safety Code Chapter 755, sets inspection intervals by the ASME construction code and requires commissioned inspectors. If your Fort Worth facility operates registered steam or hot-water boilers, our thickness data on drums, headers and tubes informs that inspector; it does not stand in for the commissioned inspection. For process plants, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) requires mechanical-integrity inspection under recognized good engineering practice.

Qualification and oversight

We have no office in Fort Worth, and technicians travel to your site for the scope. They are qualified under the Atlantis written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians set up, perform and interpret; an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Technical oversight comes from Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, and the company holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification. For operators that need a written practice or a UT procedure for a particular code, see ASNT Level III consulting and written practice development.

Typical Fort Worth UT scopes

Requests tend to follow a few patterns. A warehouse or manufacturing plant wants thickness readings on compressed-air receivers, steam lines and tanks as part of its mechanical-integrity schedule. A fabricator wants shear-wave examination of critical groove welds on structural assemblies before shipment. A gas-processing operator wants thickness surveys on separators, scrubbers and gathering piping at fixed locations, repeated each cycle so corrosion rates can be calculated. An airport or logistics campus wants a crane runway or a support structure checked after a modification. Whatever the case, we agree the locations, the procedure and the acceptance criteria first, so the data answers the question you actually have.

Repeatability is what makes thickness data useful. Locations are marked with paint or tags and drawn on an isometric so that the next survey lands on the same spots, which lets your inspector calculate corrosion rate and remaining life instead of comparing unrelated numbers.

What you receive in the UT report

The record should let a second Level II repeat the work. It lists the equipment tag and drawing, the code and procedure with revision, the instrument, probe and wedge details, the calibration blocks and their dates, the surface condition and temperature, and the technician and level. Thickness results appear as a grid with nominal and measured values and flag any location below the owner's minimum wall. Weld results include the scan plan, the reference level, and every recordable indication with position, length, amplitude and depth, followed by an accept or reject decision against the stated criteria and a sketch of the weld showing where each indication lies.

Planning UT in Fort Worth

North Texas weather swings widely. Summer steel in sun runs hot enough to affect standard probes and couplant, so outdoor work on tanks and rack piping is planned for shaded or cooler hours, and high-temperature gear is brought where lines are hot. Winter brings occasional hard freezes, when couplant thickens and surface moisture freezes into an insulating film; spring storms bring wind and rain that stop outdoor examination altogether. Allow for these when you set outage dates.

Site access is the other variable. Distribution and aviation sites at Alliance have security and badging procedures, and rail property requires its own safety training and contractor orientation before anyone goes near track. Plants have permit systems for hot work, confined space and work at height. Tell us early where the equipment is, how it is reached and what the shutdown window is, so the scope fits what can be reached and measured in the time you have.

Choosing between UT, MT and PT in Fort Worth

Use UT when the question is about wall loss, depth or internal flaws. Use magnetic particle on carbon steel when the question is a crack at the surface. Use penetrant on stainless, aluminum and other non-magnetic material. A single vessel often calls for all three, with UT for remaining wall, MT on nozzle welds and PT on stainless internals. Our MT versus PT comparison sets out the differences, and we will help you sequence the methods.

Building in-house UT capability

If you prefer your own technicians, we run UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 courses based on SNT-TC-1A hours, with theory online and practice on the UT practical simulator. Your company certifies its technicians under its own written practice, and the hands-on practical takes place at your facility. See NDT training in Fort Worth and the SNT-TC-1A eligibility tool for the experience a candidate needs.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Fort Worth?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Fort Worth. We mobilize Level II technicians to your plant, yard or facility for an agreed scope and bring the instruments, probes, blocks and couplant they need.

faq.q: What UT work do you do in Fort Worth?
faq.a: We perform contact ultrasonic thickness measurement on tanks, vessels, piping and structural steel, and angle-beam examination of welds. We do not perform radiography in the United States or any advanced ultrasonic technique.

faq.q: Can UT be used instead of radiography on welds?
faq.a: Sometimes. ASME B31.3, API 1104, AWS D1.1 and ASME Section VIII treat ultrasonic examination differently, so the owner, engineer and authorized inspector must agree the substitution before the work starts.

faq.q: How do you avoid wrong readings on corroded pipe and tanks?
faq.a: We use dual-element probes, calibrate on a step block of the same alloy, watch the A-scan for laminations and doubling, and dress a small patch to bright metal where the surface is rough. Prepared spots are recorded as such.

faq.q: Do you work on API 510, 570 and 653 equipment?
faq.a: We supply the examination data for it. The owner's authorized inspector stays responsible for the inspection and fitness decisions, and we provide thickness readings, weld data, procedures and calibration records.

faq.q: How does Texas boiler law relate to UT results?
faq.a: Texas regulates boilers through the Department of Licensing and Regulation under Health and Safety Code Chapter 755, using commissioned inspectors. Our UT data supports their decisions and does not replace their certificate inspection.

faq.q: What affects UT on hot piping?
faq.a: Standard probes and couplant have temperature limits, and sound velocity changes in hot steel. We use high-temperature probes and couplant, record the surface temperature and apply the correction in the procedure.

faq.q: How do I request a UT quote in Fort Worth?
faq.a: Use the quote form to send equipment types, code, thickness range, surface condition, access notes and your outage window. We scope the examination, state assumptions and reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can you train our technicians in ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Yes. We teach Level 1 and Level 2 ultrasonic courses built on SNT-TC-1A recommended hours, combining online theory with simulator practice. Your own company certifies the technicians and hosts the hands-on practical.

mt.title: Mag Particle Testing (MT) Inspection | Fort Worth, TX
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Fort Worth, TX for structural welds, crane and rail-yard steel, vessel and piping welds. MT to AWS and ASME. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) in Fort Worth, Texas
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Fort Worth sites for magnetic particle testing, the fast surface method for carbon and low-alloy steel. We search weld toes, lifting gear, crane structure and equipment welds for cracks that open to or lie just under the surface, and we judge them against the acceptance criteria of your code. Send the part list and specification through the quote request form and we reply within one business day.

Where mag particle testing is used in Fort Worth

Fort Worth's steel is shaped by freight, flight and fabrication. The city sits on a major freight corridor, and rail-served terminals, intermodal yards and distribution buildings across north Fort Worth run overhead cranes, container-handling gear, steel racking and heavy structural frames. Aerospace plants and their suppliers use fixtures, lifting beams, handling dollies and ground-support equipment where cracks start at welds and holes. Fabrication shops serving energy, construction and transportation produce structural frames, pressure-equipment skids and pipe supports that need final surface inspection before they ship.

The gas-field legacy of the Barnett Shale adds separators, compressor skids, wellhead structures and gathering-line fittings, mostly carbon steel and mostly good MT candidates. Industrial buildings, bridge-related steel and municipal structures add the structural side. In every case the target is the same: a fatigue or fabrication crack that has started at a weld toe, a notch or a threaded section, long before it is visible, and that magnetic particles can reveal.

The physics, and its limits

A magnetized steel part carries flux lines through its volume. A crack that crosses those lines forces some flux out of the surface, and fine iron particles collect over the leakage as a sharp, visible line. This explains both the strengths and the boundaries of the method. Particles show the crack that crosses the field, not the one that runs along it. The method needs ferromagnetic material, so it works on carbon and most low-alloy steels but not on austenitic stainless, aluminum or copper. It is a surface and near-surface method; deeper flaws do not leak enough flux to hold particles.

  • Orientation: the part is examined twice with the field turned about ninety degrees, so any crack direction is caught.
  • Coating thickness: thick paint spaces the particles from the surface and weakens indications, so coating is removed or the procedure is qualified for it.
  • Geometry: sharp threads and section changes can leak flux with no flaw present, which produces non-relevant indications that a Level II must interpret.

For internal flaws and wall loss, ultrasonic testing in Fort Worth is the right companion; for stainless and aluminum parts, use penetrant testing in Fort Worth.

Technique in the field

For most Fort Worth work we use portable electromagnetic yokes. The yoke is placed across the weld with its legs on either side, magnetizing the joint between them. ASME Section V Article 7 expects an AC yoke to lift at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing in use, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, and the lift is checked with a test weight before work. Particles are applied while the field is on; after the first pass the yoke is rotated for the second pass at roughly right angles.

The choice of particles depends on surface and sensitivity. Dry powder is convenient on rough or warm steel; visible wet particles in a carrier give a cleaner picture on smoother surfaces; fluorescent wet particles give the highest sensitivity under UV-A light, provided the viewing area is dark enough and the light intensity is verified. Central conductor or coil techniques magnetize shafts and bars, and prods can magnetize large welds in locations where arc burns are acceptable. When residual magnetism could affect service or later welding, the part is demagnetized and checked with a field meter. See our complete MT guide and the Article 7 explainer.

Applicable codes and Texas context

MT acceptance depends on the construction code. Pressure vessels under ASME Section VIII Division 1 use Appendix 6; process piping under ASME B31.3 uses paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2; power piping falls under B31.1. Structural steel under AWS D1.1 and bridge steel under AWS D1.5 call for visual and magnetic particle examination with their own acceptance tables, and ASTM E709 and E1444 supply the guide and practice most procedures draw from. Where equipment is in service under API 510, 570 or 653, the owner's authorized inspector decides what to do about a crack; we locate, size and document it.

Texas has a statutory boiler program run by the Department of Licensing and Regulation under Health and Safety Code Chapter 755; repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code, with commissioned inspectors signing off. MT on a header weld repair or a lifting-lug weld becomes part of that file. For plants under process safety management, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) makes inspection of equipment, including crack detection, part of the mechanical-integrity program.

Who does the examination

We have no office in Fort Worth, so technicians travel to your site. They are qualified under the Atlantis written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A: Level II performs and interprets, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Technical oversight rests with Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certificates cover the Atlantis management system. If you need a procedure written to your specification, Level III consulting can supply it.

Reading the particles: real cracks and false alarms

Particles gather wherever flux leaks, and not every leak is a crack. A relevant indication comes from a real discontinuity such as a crack, lap or lack of fusion. Non-relevant indications come from magnetic writing, abrupt thickness changes, thread roots and the boundary between weld metal and base metal. Poorly cleaned surfaces and excess current can leave false indications. A Level II technician will lightly clean, re-magnetize and re-examine a questionable line, then record the decision. The report notes the cause, because an inspector reading it later needs to know whether a line was dismissed for a reason or simply missed.

Surface condition therefore matters before any particles go on. Loose scale, weld spatter and grease are removed; painted surfaces are treated according to the coating limits in the procedure; and in outdoor work the area is dry. On old structures, welds under years of paint may need local coating removal before MT, and the owner should plan the touch-up afterwards.

Typical Fort Worth MT scopes

Most MT requests come from a few situations. A fabricator wants final magnetic particle examination of structural welds before shipment. A distribution or manufacturing site wants periodic inspection of crane hooks, runway welds and lifting beams under its rigging program. A vessel repair crew needs MT of a ground-out excavation before the repair weld and of the finished repair afterwards. A gas facility wants MT on skid-frame welds, nozzle attachments and pipe-support welds during a shutdown. Each job is sized by the number of welds or parts, the access, and the procedure, and each ends with a report your own inspector or engineer can file.

When you ask for a quote, tell us the thickness of any coating, the material grade and whether the work is new construction or in service. Those three details change the technique more than anything else, and they let us bring the right yoke, the right particles and the right surface preparation tools on the first visit.

What the MT report contains

Each report names the component and tag, the code and the procedure with revision, the equipment and its last lifting-power check, the particle type and carrier, the magnetizing technique and field direction, the light levels for fluorescent work, the surface condition and part temperature, and the technician and level. Every indication is located on a sketch, with its type, orientation and length, and is marked relevant or non-relevant and accepted or rejected against the named criteria. If the part was demagnetized, the residual field reading is included, and photographs can support a disputed call.

Planning MT in Fort Worth

Weather decides the method. In a North Texas summer, steel in the sun can be too hot for liquid carriers, which evaporate before the examination is complete; we plan shaded or cooler periods or switch to dry powder where that is allowed. Wind makes dry powder awkward, and a screen or a changed schedule may be needed. Winter mornings can be cold and damp, and moisture on the surface hurts contrast. Fluorescent work needs darkness, which is easy in a building and harder on an open yard, where a portable shroud or after-dark access may be needed.

Access planning matters as much. Facilities at AllianceTexas and elsewhere have badging and orientation steps, rail property requires contractor safety training, and plants require permits for hot work, confined space and height. Cranes and elevated structure need access equipment arranged beforehand; a yoke inspection is only as good as the reach. Share your dates and access constraints with your quote request.

Surface preparation and demagnetization in practice

Good MT starts before the yoke comes out. We remove loose scale, spatter and oil with wire brushes or light grinding, and we check any coating with a thickness gauge against the limit in the procedure. On old rail-yard and plant structure, welds hidden under years of paint often need a clean window at each joint. Afterwards, if the part will be welded, machined or placed near sensitive equipment, we demagnetize it by stepping down an alternating field and confirm the residual reading with a meter, so the magnetism does not deflect a later welding arc or hold chips to a finished surface.

Wet methods leave residue as well, so cleanup is part of the scope: carrier and particles are wiped from the area, and the surface is left ready for coating repair by your crew.

MT, PT or UT for Fort Worth jobs

For a surface crack in carbon steel, MT is fast and sensitive. For stainless, aluminum or any non-magnetic alloy, use penetrant. For depth, wall loss or internal flaws, add ultrasonic examination. The MT versus PT comparison explains the differences in more detail, and the national magnetic particle testing page describes our scope.

Training your own MT technicians

We train candidates in MT Level 1 and MT Level 2, following SNT-TC-1A recommended hours, with online theory and practice questions in the NDT practice tests. Your company certifies its own technicians and runs the practical at your facility. Learn more on the Fort Worth NDT training page.

faq.q: Do you have an office in Fort Worth?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Fort Worth. We mobilize Level II technicians to your site with yokes, particles, light meters and test weights for the agreed magnetic particle scope.

faq.q: Which metals can be inspected by magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Only ferromagnetic metals such as carbon steel, most low-alloy steels and martensitic grades. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper cannot be magnetized, so they need liquid penetrant testing for surface cracks.

faq.q: Why do you examine each weld twice?
faq.a: A crack running parallel to the magnetic field barely disturbs it. Examining with the field turned about ninety degrees, as ASME Section V Article 7 requires, ensures cracks of any direction can be detected.

faq.q: Can you inspect crane hooks, lugs and handling gear?
faq.a: Yes. Hooks, shackles, lifting lugs, spreader bars and their attachment welds are routine MT subjects. We examine to your procedure, and the owner or rigging authority decides on any component that shows a crack.

faq.q: What do fluorescent particles add?
faq.a: Fluorescent particles under UV-A light show fine cracks more clearly than visible particles. They need a darkened area and checked light levels, which we verify against the procedure before examining.

faq.q: Does every part need demagnetizing afterwards?
faq.a: No. Demagnetizing is done when residual magnetism could interfere with service, welding or machining, or when the specification calls for it. The residual field reading is recorded when it is done.

faq.q: Do you provide API authorized inspectors?
faq.a: No. Under API 510, 570 and 653 the inspector of record is the one the owner names. Atlantis performs the MT examination and hands over indication data and records for that person to evaluate.

faq.q: How do I request MT in Fort Worth?
faq.a: Send the part list, material, code, surface condition, access notes and outage dates through the quote form. We scope the work, set out assumptions and reply within one business day.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) | Fort Worth, TX Dye Check
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Fort Worth, TX for stainless and aluminum welds, aerospace tooling, vessels and piping. Visible or fluorescent. Get a quote.
pt.h1: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Fort Worth, Texas
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Fort Worth sites to perform liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant or PT. It finds cracks, laps and porosity that are open to the surface of any non-porous material, which makes it the surface method for stainless steel, aluminum, titanium and nickel alloys, as well as for carbon steel when yoke access is awkward. Describe the parts and the code with the quote request form and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Fort Worth

Penetrant suits Fort Worth because so much of its industry works in non-magnetic alloys. Aerospace and defense manufacturing and maintenance rely on aluminum, titanium and nickel-alloy structure and on the tooling, fixtures and ground-support equipment that serve it. Maintenance and overhaul activity at the airports adds welded repairs and fabricated brackets. Process equipment for food, beverage and chemical plants in the metroplex is frequently stainless, and the transportation sector, from rail equipment shops to truck and automotive suppliers, uses welded aluminum and stainless components.

Penetrant is also useful on the energy side. Barnett Shale compression and gas-processing facilities use stainless small-bore tubing, instrument connections and valve bodies, where a penetrant check after repair welding or machining is practical. Heat exchanger tubesheet welds, socket welds and weld-overlay repairs are all routine PT subjects. It is also the method of choice on a ground-out crack excavation, where the question is whether any crack is left open to the surface before welding resumes.

What PT finds, and what it cannot

The mechanism is capillary action. Penetrant on a clean surface is drawn into any surface-breaking discontinuity, held there while excess is removed, and then pulled out by a developer into a visible indication. The reach of the method is wide because it needs no magnetic property, but its blind spots are firm. A flaw that does not open to the surface is invisible to PT. A crack plugged by oil, oxide, paint or smeared metal cannot take penetrant. A porous or rough surface soaks up penetrant everywhere and drowns the signal in background.

  • Mechanical cleaning side effects: blasting, grinding or wire brushing can peen over a crack mouth, so etching or a controlled preparation step may be needed.
  • Chemical compatibility: penetrant materials used on stainless and nickel alloys must be low in halogens and sulfur, which is checked on the certificate for each lot.
  • Surface temperature: out of range, the liquids misbehave, and the procedure has to be qualified for the temperature.

When the question is depth or wall loss, use ultrasonic testing in Fort Worth; for carbon-steel weld toes, magnetic particle testing in Fort Worth is often faster.

The technique, step by step

Procedures set the penetrant type and removal method. Type I fluorescent penetrants are examined under UV-A light in a dark area and detect finer cracks; Type II visible penetrants are viewed in white light and suit field use. Method A is water washable, Method B uses an emulsifier, and Method C uses solvent removal, which is the typical field approach because it needs only cleaner and wipes. The governing practices are ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165.

The steps are always the same in order. Clean and dry the surface. Apply penetrant by spray or brush and keep it wet for the dwell time in the procedure. Remove the excess with care, because wiping too hard removes penetrant from the flaw, while wiping too little leaves a background. Apply a thin even layer of developer, allow the developing time, then examine in adequate light. The technician interprets indications during the developing window and records them. Our penetrant testing simulator demonstrates the sequence, and the national penetrant testing page gives the scope.

Codes and Texas requirements

Acceptance comes from the construction code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 sets PT methods and acceptance for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 do the same for process piping, and AWS D1.1 and D1.6 apply to structural carbon and stainless steel. For in-service vessels and piping under API 510 and 570, the owner's authorized inspector decides about fitness; our role is to find and record the surface indications with their location and size.

The Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation runs the boiler program under Health and Safety Code Chapter 755, with commissioned inspectors and National Board rules for repair and alteration. A penetrant result on a header repair or tube-to-tubesheet weld becomes part of the evidence they rely on. Plants under process safety management carry the OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j) duty to inspect equipment under good engineering practice, which is where regular PT on stainless components often fits.

Who performs penetrant testing for us

Atlantis has no office in Fort Worth; technicians travel to your site. They work under the Atlantis written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with Level II performing and interpreting and an ASNT Level III approving the technique and reviewing reports. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, provides technical oversight. The management system is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If you need a penetrant procedure for your materials, Level III consulting can write it.

Interpreting bleed-out

A stain on the developer is not always a flaw. Indications whose length is at least three times the width are normally treated as linear, which points to cracks, laps and seams; rounded indications suggest porosity or pits; a diffuse stain usually signals poor removal. The technician watches indications develop, because a crack that keeps bleeding grows quickly while a trapped residue does not. Doubtful indications are wiped and re-developed once when the procedure allows. Non-relevant indications, such as penetrant held in a weld toe notch, are documented and explained rather than left unexplained.

Consistency matters across the whole job. Using the same penetrant family, dwell and lighting for every weld keeps results comparable. In fluorescent work the technician lets his eyes adapt in the dark area, and in visible work he checks light levels at the surface. Consumables are kept sealed and replaced if contaminated with water or dirt.

Typical Fort Worth penetrant scopes

Common requests are easy to describe. A fabricator wants final PT on stainless skid welds before delivery. An aircraft-related shop wants a surface check on a repaired aluminum fixture or a machined part. A processing plant wants stainless weld repairs on a vessel or heat exchanger verified before return to service. A gas facility wants PT on socket welds and small-bore connections after modifications. A repair contractor wants a ground-out crack excavation checked before welding resumes and the finished repair checked after it cools. Each scope is sized by the surface area, number of welds, cleaning needed and access.

Timing with the welder matters because many penetrant jobs are repairs. A repair weld is examined after it cools into the temperature range of the procedure, and an excavation is examined before welding, so the crew knows the crack is gone. We coordinate with your welding foreman, and we leave the area clean of developer residue that could contaminate the next weld pass if left in a groove.

What the PT report contains

A PT report documents the process as well as the result. It lists the component and weld, the code and procedure revision, the penetrant, remover and developer by manufacturer and lot, the sensitivity level and method, the cleaning agents, the part and ambient temperature, the dwell and developing times, and the measured lighting. Each indication is described by shape, size, orientation and position, shown on a sketch or photograph, and accepted or rejected against the criteria named. Lot records for sulfur and halogen content are kept for work on stainless and nickel alloys.

Planning penetrant work in Fort Worth

The standard temperature range in ASME Section V Article 6 for the part and the penetrant materials is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside it the procedure must be qualified. North Texas summers carry sun-heated steel well above that, which flashes off solvent and developer, and winter cold snaps can fall below it. We measure the part temperature with a contact thermometer, schedule outdoor work for the right part of the day, and cool or warm the part when required. Spring wind and rain stop outdoor work; dust sticks to wet penetrant.

Plan site access in advance. Airport and logistics campuses have security and badging steps, rail property requires contractor safety training, and plants have permits for confined space, hot work and height. Process areas restrict solvents near ignition sources, so we have the cleaner and developer approved before they arrive. Tell us the surface condition, the cleaning needed and the outage dates in your quote request so the preparation is properly scoped.

Cleaning, removal and developer: where results are won

Most penetrant failures trace to cleaning. We degrease with solvent, remove paint and scale mechanically or chemically as the procedure requires, and then let the surface dry fully, since solvent trapped in a crack blocks penetrant just as oil does. After dwell, solvent-removable penetrant is wiped with clean dry cloths first, then with a cloth lightly dampened with remover, never flooded, which would wash penetrant out of shallow cracks. Developer is applied in a thin, even coat from the correct distance, because a thick coat masks fine indications.

When the job is finished, residue is wiped off and the part is post-cleaned if the procedure requires it, which matters for parts that will be welded or placed in service with sensitive fluids.

Choosing the penetrant system

The penetrant system is chosen to match the job. Fluorescent penetrant is the usual choice for critical welds and fine cracks, provided a dark area can be arranged. Visible penetrant works in daylight and shop light and is the practical choice for most field repairs. Higher-sensitivity systems find tighter cracks but also pick up more background on rough surfaces, so the procedure balances sensitivity against surface finish. Tell us the material, finish and acceptance level when you ask for the quote and we will state which system we plan to use.

PT, MT or UT for Fort Worth jobs

Choose penetrant for non-magnetic alloys, small or awkward geometry, and a clear answer on open flaws. Choose magnetic particle for carbon steel when speed and sensitivity matter. Choose ultrasonic when the concern lies below the surface. See the MT versus PT comparison and the Article 6 explainer for details.

Training penetrant technicians

For an in-house program, see PT Level 1 and PT Level 2, with online theory and simulator practice. Your company certifies its technicians and runs the practical at its own facility. Details are on the Fort Worth NDT training page.

faq.q: Do you have an office or lab in Fort Worth?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office or lab in Fort Worth. We mobilize Level II technicians to your site with the penetrant materials, thermometers and light meters needed for the agreed scope.

faq.q: What does penetrant testing detect?
faq.a: Only flaws that are open to the surface, such as cracks, laps, seams and porosity, on non-porous material. Subsurface flaws and cracks blocked by paint, oil or oxide will not show unless cleaning opens them.

faq.q: Which materials need penetrant rather than magnetic particle?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steel, duplex alloys, aluminum, titanium, copper and nickel alloys are not magnetic, so penetrant is the surface method for them. It also helps on carbon steel where yoke access is awkward.

faq.q: What temperature range applies to penetrant testing?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 gives 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the penetrant materials. Beyond that the procedure must be qualified for the temperature, and we measure the surface temperature on the day.

faq.q: Why is cleaning so important?
faq.a: Penetrant cannot enter a crack blocked by grease, oxide, paint or smeared metal. Poor cleaning hides real flaws, and poor removal leaves a background that makes indications hard to judge.

faq.q: Can you test stainless steel and aluminum welds?
faq.a: Yes. Those are the common penetrant subjects. We use materials suitable for the alloy, including low-halogen and low-sulfur products on stainless and nickel alloys, and report indications against the code or specification.

faq.q: Does Atlantis supply API authorized inspectors?
faq.a: No. On API 510, 570 and 653 equipment, the owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record. Our job is the penetrant examination itself, with indications and records documented for that inspector to use.

faq.a: Use the quote form to tell us what you have, which code applies, how the surface looks, where it sits and when it can be shut down. We scope the work, state assumptions and reply within one business day.
